topic.title: Sperm, fertilisation, implantation and the placenta
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: On Summer 2025's Higher paper this was Q6, and its last four parts were the ones the report singled out: the zygote confused with the embryo, and implantation confused with differentiation. It usually carries 6 to 9 marks as a chain of one-mark recall parts, plus a three-mark 'explain how the placenta is adapted' part that is marked as feature-plus-consequence pairs.
mustMemorise: Sperm: made by meiosis; haploid nucleus, mitochondria for energy (Higher), flagellum for swimming
Fertilisation happens in the oviduct: two haploid nuclei fuse to give a diploid zygote
Zygote (one cell) → mitosis → ball of cells → implantation in the uterus LINING → differentiation
Implantation is a change of place; differentiation is a change of job
Placenta: large surface area from the villi, thin barrier, good blood supply
In to the foetus: dissolved nutrients and oxygen. Out: carbon dioxide and urea
The umbilical cord carries the blood; the amnion is the membrane round the foetus, and the fluid inside it cushions the foetus
notOnThisSpec: The acrosome, and the change in the egg membrane that stops a second sperm
Blastocyst, trophoblast, chorion and decidua as terms (CCEA says 'ball of cells')
The corpus luteum, hCG and pregnancy testing

mustBeAbleTo: Name the three adaptations of a sperm cell and give the reason for each
State that sperm are formed by meiosis and that the nucleus is haploid
Name the oviduct as the site of fertilisation, and say that two haploid nuclei fuse to give a diploid zygote
Tell a zygote (one cell) from an embryo (many cells) in one sentence
Tell implantation (a change of place) from differentiation (a change of job) in one sentence
Say that implantation happens in the LINING, naming the layer and not only the organ
Explain how the placenta is adapted for diffusion, as feature-plus-consequence pairs
Name what crosses the placenta in each direction: nutrients and oxygen in, carbon dioxide and urea out
Explain the role of the villi (Higher Tier) and of the mitochondria in a sperm (Higher Tier)

sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. This content usually carries a whole question of 6 to 9 marks, built as a chain of one-mark recall parts that walk down the same sequence: where fertilisation happens, what the cell is called, where it implants, what happens next. Summer 2025's Higher paper put five of those parts in a row. The placenta appears as a three-mark 'explain how it is adapted' part, marked as feature-plus-consequence pairs, and the data parts come from Unit 7 Booklet B.
traps: Writing 'embryo' for the single cell formed when the two nuclei fuse: that cell is a zygote, and it is an embryo only once it has divided (Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q6)

Using the word differentiation without being able to say what it means — the examiners reported that the concept was not understood here, and the mark is for cells taking on different jobs (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q6)
Saying the flagellum moves, rather than saying what it does for the cell: the mark is for it letting the sperm swim (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q1)
Giving a feature of the placenta without what it does, or no feature at all: fewer candidates earned the mark for how the placenta is adapted (Summer 2024 B2 Foundation Q3(b)(ii))
Using implantation where differentiation was meant, and the other way round (Summer 2025 B2 Higher)
Answering 'the uterus' where the scheme wants 'the lining of the uterus' (Summer 2024 B2 Higher)
Writing that the mother's blood flows into the foetus
Giving a bare 'large surface area' with no consequence in a three-mark placenta question
Saying the amniotic fluid feeds the foetus
Dividing time by distance in a speed calculation
Adding two to the number of divisions instead of doubling the number of cells

workedExamples.stem: A zygote divides by mitosis. Calculate how many cells are in the ball after 6 divisions. [2]

data.caption: Cells in the ball after each division by mitosis

steps.working: Read the pattern off the table: 2, 4, 8, 16.
steps.decision: Each row is double the row above it. Name the pattern before you carry it on, because that is what the first mark is for.

options: Because mitosis makes each cell into two
Because the cells get bigger each time
Because one new cell is added each time
whyMenu.explain: Mitosis makes two cells from one, so the count doubles. It does not add one, and the cells do not grow between divisions — which is why the ball stays the same size.

steps.working: Carry the doubling on: 32 after 5 divisions, 64 after 6.
steps.decision: Two doublings past the printed table. Writing the intermediate value down is what stops an off-by-one slip.
Check the row you were asked for. The commonest wrong answers here are one doubling short and the number of divisions doubled.

twin.stem: How many cells are in the ball after 5 divisions?

steps.working: Recognise the question: this is an exchange surface, like the alveolus and the root hair.
steps.decision: The same four points answer all of them: a large surface area, a thin barrier, a good blood supply, and a difference in concentration that is kept up.

steps.working: The villi give a large surface area, so more substances diffuse at once.
steps.decision: A feature on its own is not a marking point. Each mark is the feature plus what it does.

options: Because a bare 'large surface area' does not say what it achieves
Because the villi are the only part that matters
Because surface area is always worth two marks
whyMenu.explain: Structure plus consequence is the pattern in every exchange-surface scheme. Write the 'so…' half in the same sentence.

steps.working: The barrier between the two blood supplies is thin, so the diffusion distance is short.
steps.decision: Thin is only half the point; the short distance is the other half.

steps.working: Both sides have a good blood supply, which keeps the difference in concentration up.
steps.decision: Blood flow carries the arriving substance away, so the difference never evens out and diffusion keeps going.

steps.working: Check: the answer never says the two bloods mix.
steps.decision: They come close but never join — that is why diffusion is needed at all.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The villi give a large surface area, so more diffusion happens at once; the barrier is thin, so the distance to diffuse is short; and the good blood supply on both sides keeps the difference in concentration up.

twin.stem: Name the part of the placenta that gives it its large surface area.

workedExamples.stem:
In IVF, an embryo is placed in the uterus once the zygote has divided into a ball of 128 cells.
(a) How many times has the zygote divided? [1]
(b) Name the process that made these divisions, and give one feature of the cells it makes. [2]

steps.decision: Each division doubles the cells, so n divisions make 2 to the power n. Find the power of 2 that gives 128. Halving 128 is a different sum.

options: Because each division doubles the number of cells
Because each division adds two cells
Because the cells grow between divisions
whyMenu.explain: Every cell in the ball divides into two, so each division doubles the count.

steps.decision: The zygote's divisions are mitosis; meiosis made the sperm and the egg.
Mitosis copies the cell: every cell in the ball carries the same chromosomes.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 7. (b) Mitosis; the cells are genetically identical.

twin.stem: How many times must a zygote divide by mitosis to make a ball of 512 cells?

workedExamples.stem:
A foetus had a mass of 600 g at 24 weeks and 2600 g at 34 weeks.
(a) Calculate how many grams it gained, on average, each week. [3]
(b) Name the structure that carries the nutrients for this growth from the placenta to the foetus. [1]

steps.decision: The change in mass first: the end value minus the start.
Then the time it took, also a subtraction. Dividing by the week number itself is the usual slip.
A rate is the change divided by the time.

options: Because a mean rate is the total change divided by the time
Because the mass must be multiplied by the weeks
Because only the last mass matters
whyMenu.explain: Grams per week means grams divided by weeks: the total gain spread over the time.

steps.decision: Nutrients cross the placenta into the foetus's blood, which runs to the foetus through the cord.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 200 g per week. (b) The umbilical cord.

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have already met. In which part of the female reproductive system does fertilisation take place?
items.skill: Recall the site of fertilisation (previous topic)

options.feedback: The oviduct. Everything in this topic happens along the route from there to the uterus.
The uterus is the destination, not the place the nuclei fuse.
The ovary releases the ovum; fertilisation happens after it has left.
The cervix is the ring of muscle at the base of the uterus.

items.stem: Which structure in a cell releases energy by respiration?

options.feedback: The mitochondria. A sperm cell is packed with them, and you will see why shortly.
The nucleus holds the chromosomes.
The membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Most reactions happen in the cytoplasm, but respiration that needs oxygen happens inside the mitochondria.

items.stem: A group of cells of the same kind working together is called a…

options.feedback: A tissue. Differentiation, later in this lesson, is how a ball of identical cells ends up with tissues in it.
An organ is made of several tissues.
An organ system is a group of organs.
An organism is the whole living thing.

items.stem: A single cell is formed when a sperm nucleus and an egg nucleus fuse. What is that cell called?
items.skill: Tell a zygote from an embryo

options.feedback: A zygote — one cell, and diploid.
An embryo is many cells. This one has not divided yet.
The gametes were the sperm and the ovum, before they fused.
A foetus is much later, once the organs have formed.

items.stem: A ball of cells sinks into the thickened lining of the uterus. What is this called?

options.feedback: Implantation: a change of place.
Differentiation is a change of job — the cells becoming different from one another. It comes after implantation.
Fertilisation happened days earlier, in the oviduct.
Ovulation is the release of the ovum from the ovary.

items.stem: The cells of a ball of cells begin to become different from one another, forming tissues. What is this called?

options.feedback: Differentiation: a change of job.
Implantation is the ball settling into the lining — a change of place, not of job.
Mitosis makes more cells, all identical. Differentiation is what makes them different.
Fertilisation is the fusing of two nuclei.

items.stem: Which type of cell division makes sperm?

options.feedback: Meiosis. It halves the chromosome number, which is why the sperm nucleus is haploid.
Mitosis makes identical diploid cells. If gametes were made by mitosis the chromosome number would double at every fertilisation.
Differentiation is cells becoming specialised, not a type of division.
Fertilisation joins two cells rather than dividing one.

items.stem: Which pair of substances crosses the placenta from the mother's blood into the blood of the foetus?
items.skill: Know which way each substance crosses

options.feedback: Oxygen and dissolved nutrients go in; carbon dioxide and urea come back.
Those are the two wastes, and they travel the other way.
Oxygen goes in, but urea is a waste from the foetus and comes out.
The two blood supplies never mix, so blood cells do not cross.

items.stem: What is the function of the amniotic fluid?
items.skill: Give the job of the amniotic fluid

options.feedback: It cushions the foetus against knocks.

options.text: it supplies the foetus with food
options.feedback: Food reaches the foetus through the placenta and the umbilical cord.

options.text: it supplies the foetus with oxygen
options.feedback: Oxygen also crosses the placenta; the fluid carries none of it.

options.text: it carries waste away from the foetus
options.feedback: Waste leaves through the umbilical cord and the placenta.

items.stem: A zygote has divided 6 times by mitosis. How many cells are there?

options.feedback: 64. Each division doubles the count: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.
That doubles the number of divisions rather than the number of cells.
That is one doubling short. Count the divisions again.
That squares the number of divisions. It is two that is multiplied by itself each time.

parts.stem: Name the structures labelled (i) and (iii) on the diagram of the sperm cell.
parts.workedSolution: (i) is the haploid nucleus and (iii) is the flagellum.

hints: Say what it lets the cell do, not what it looks like.

it allows the sperm to swim
the flagellum lets the sperm swim towards the ovum

hints: They are the structures packed into the middle piece.
parts.stem: Name the structures labelled (ii) on the diagram of the sperm cell.
parts.workedSolution: (ii) are the mitochondria.

hints: Two steps: what the mitochondria do, and what the cell spends it on.

commonErrors.feedback: Energy is not made. Mitochondria release energy that was already stored in glucose, by respiration — the scheme reads for the word release.

parts.stem: Explain why a sperm cell has so many of the structures labelled (ii).

accepted: the mitochondria release energy by respiration, and that energy is used to move the flagellum so the sperm can swim to the ovum

scheme.for: the energy is used to move the flagellum, so the sperm can swim

parts.workedSolution: The mitochondria release energy by respiration, and that energy is used to move the flagellum so the sperm can swim to the ovum.

context.setting: Chromosome numbers in a gamete and in a zygote

hints: A gamete carries one chromosome of each pair.

commonErrors.feedback: 46 is the diploid number, the number in a body cell. A gamete is haploid: it carries one chromosome of each pair, so half that number.

parts.stem:
A human body cell contains 46 chromosomes.
How many chromosomes are there in the nucleus of a human sperm cell?
parts.workedSolution: A sperm is haploid, so it carries half of 46, which is 23 chromosomes.

hints: Two haploid nuclei fuse into one.

commonErrors.feedback: 23 is the haploid number that each gamete brings. Fertilisation puts the two sets together, so the zygote is diploid.

parts.stem: How many chromosomes are there in the nucleus of the zygote formed when that sperm fertilises an ovum?
parts.workedSolution: The haploid sperm nucleus and the haploid egg nucleus fuse, so 23 + 23 = 46. The zygote is diploid.
parts.noFollowThrough: Scheme line: 46. The zygote's number is the body cell's number the stem gives, not a value carried from part (a).

context.setting: Counting the cells in the ball as the zygote divides

data.caption: Cells in the ball after each division by mitosis

hints: Each division doubles the number of cells.
Carry the doubling on past the last printed row.

commonErrors.feedback: That doubles the number of divisions instead of the number of cells. The cells double each time, so the count goes 2, 4, 8, 16 — not 2, 4, 6, 8.
That is the count after one division fewer. Read the row you were asked for and check you have doubled the right number of times.
That squares the number of divisions. It is two that is multiplied by itself each time, not the number of divisions.

parts.stem:
The table shows how many cells a zygote has produced after each division by mitosis.
Calculate the number of cells after 6 divisions.

scheme.for: continues the doubling past the printed rows: 2, 4, 8, 16, …

parts.workedSolution: Every division doubles the number of cells: 2, 4, 8, 16, then 32, then 64. So after 6 divisions there are 64 cells. The ball is no bigger than the zygote was — the cells simply get smaller.

context.setting: Putting the four events between ovulation and a growing embryo into order

hints: Nothing can be fertilised before it has been released.
The ball of cells has to settle somewhere before its cells can start to become different.

commonErrors.feedback: Differentiation comes last. Implantation is a change of place — the ball settles into the lining; differentiation is a change of job — the cells become different from each other.

parts.stem: Put these four events in the order they happen, starting with the earliest.
parts.workedSolution: Ovulation, fertilisation, implantation, differentiation. The ovary releases the ovum; the nuclei fuse in the oviduct; the ball of cells settles into the uterus lining; and only then do its cells begin to become different from one another.

context.setting: Where each stage of early development happens

hints: It happens on the way, not at either end.

commonErrors.feedback: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct, as the ovum travels. The uterus is where the ball of cells implants afterwards, and the ovary is where the ovum came from.

parts.stem: Name the part of the female reproductive system in which fertilisation takes place.
parts.workedSolution: In the oviduct.

hints: The word uterus on its own was not enough for the mark.

commonErrors.feedback: The uterus alone was not enough for this mark. The ball of cells embeds itself in the lining, the thickened layer on the inside of the uterus wall.

parts.stem: State exactly where in the uterus the ball of cells implants.

accepted: in the lining of the uterus

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 Higher: naming the organ alone was not enough here, because the scheme asked for the layer inside it.

parts.workedSolution: In the lining of the uterus.

context.setting: Telling the four events of early development apart

hints: Count the cells: that is the whole difference.

commonErrors.feedback: The two are the wrong way round. One cell is a zygote; many cells is an embryo. Summer 2025's report names this swap as one of the two commonest losses on this question.

parts.stem:
A zygote and an embryo are not the same thing.
Explain the difference between them.

accepted: a zygote is the single cell made when the two nuclei fuse, and an embryo is the many cells that form once that zygote has divided by mitosis

any: embryo is a ball of cells
embryo is made of many cells

scheme.for: a zygote is one cell, formed when the sperm and egg nuclei fuse
an embryo is many cells, formed after the zygote has divided by mitosis

parts.workedSolution: A zygote is the single cell made when the two nuclei fuse, and an embryo is the many cells that form once that zygote has divided by mitosis. If you can count the cells and the answer is one, it is a zygote.

hints: One is about where the ball of cells is; the other is about what its cells are becoming.

commonErrors.feedback: The two words have swapped jobs. Implantation is a change of place — the ball of cells settles into the lining. Differentiation is a change of job — the cells become different from one another.

parts.stem: Explain the difference between implantation and differentiation.

accepted: implantation is when the ball of cells settles into the lining of the uterus, and differentiation is when its cells become different from one another to make tissues and organs

any: implantation is when the ball of cells settles
implantation is the ball of cells settling
implantation is when the embryo settles
implantation is when the ball of cells embeds
implantation is when the embryo sinks into the lining
implantation is when it attaches to the lining
differentiation is when its cells become different
differentiation is when the cells become different
differentiation is when cells become different
differentiation is the cells becoming different
differentiation is when cells become specialised
differentiation is when the cells become specialised

scheme.for: implantation: the ball of cells settles into (embeds in) the lining of the uterus — a change of place
differentiation: the cells become different from one another, forming tissues and organs — a change of job

parts.workedSolution: Implantation is when the ball of cells settles into the lining of the uterus, and differentiation is when its cells become different from one another to make tissues and organs. Implantation is a change of place; differentiation is a change of job.

context.setting: Comparing glucose concentrations either side of the placenta

parts.stem:
Blood in the mother's side of a placenta carried 5.4 mmol/dm³ of glucose. Blood in the umbilical vein leaving the placenta carried 3.6 mmol/dm³.
Calculate the percentage drop in glucose concentration across the placenta.
Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.workedSolution: The drop is 5.4 − 3.6 = 1.8 mmol/dm³. As a percentage of the starting concentration: 1.8 ÷ 5.4 × 100 = 33.3%. The concentrations are different because glucose is diffusing across, and that difference is what keeps the diffusion going.

parts.stem:
Under a microscope, one sperm cell swam 4.8 mm across a dish in 3.0 minutes.

parts.workedSolution: Speed = distance ÷ time = 4.8 ÷ 3.0 = 1.6 mm per minute.

hints: Rearranging speed = distance ÷ time gives time = distance ÷ speed.

parts.stem:
The oviduct in this dish measures 96 mm.

parts.workedSolution: Time = distance ÷ speed = 96 ÷ 1.6 = 60 minutes.

parts.stem:
Describe what happens from the moment a sperm reaches an ovum until the cells of the embryo begin to differentiate.
Use the words zygote, mitosis, implantation and differentiation in your answer.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

keyWords: fertilisation takes place in the oviduct
reaches the ovum in the oviduct

indicativeContent.point: the haploid nuclei of the sperm and the ovum fuse
the cell that results is a diploid zygote — a single cell
the zygote divides by mitosis, many times
this makes a ball of identical cells, which travels down the oviduct to the uterus
keyWords: down the oviduct to the uterus

indicativeContent.point: the ball of cells implants in the lining of the uterus
after implantation the cells differentiate, forming tissues and organs

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: The two losses the Summer 2025 report names are both about words: the zygote called an embryo (one cell against many), and implantation used where differentiation was meant (a change of place against a change of job). An answer that has the events in the right order but calls them by the wrong names caps at Band B. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

parts.workedSolution: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct. The haploid nucleus of the sperm and the haploid nucleus of the ovum fuse, and the single cell that results is a diploid zygote. That zygote then divides by mitosis, over and over, making a ball of identical cells while it travels down the oviduct towards the uterus. The ball of cells implants in the lining of the uterus, sinking into the thickened layer there. Only after implantation do the cells differentiate, becoming different from one another to form the tissues and organs of the embryo.

context.setting: Five stages of early pregnancy described in a leaflet, each to be named

parts.stem:
A leaflet describes five stages of early pregnancy. Stage 1: a sperm reaches an ovum in the oviduct. Stage 2: a single cell forms. Stage 3: a ball of identical cells forms. Stage 4: the ball sinks into the uterus lining. Stage 5: the cells form tissues and organs.
Name the single cell formed at stage 2.
hints: Name it: one word is enough.
parts.workedSolution: A zygote.

commonErrors.feedback: One cell is a zygote. It becomes an embryo only once it has divided into a ball of many cells.

parts.stem: At stage 3 the single cell has become a ball of identical cells. Name this ball of cells.
hints: Name it: one word is enough.
parts.workedSolution: An embryo.

commonErrors.feedback: A zygote is the single cell. Once it has divided into a ball of many identical cells, it is an embryo.

parts.stem: Name the type of cell division that turns the single cell into the ball of cells.
hints: Name it: one word is enough.
parts.workedSolution: Mitosis.

commonErrors.feedback: Meiosis made the sperm and the egg. The zygote's divisions make identical cells, so they are mitosis.

parts.stem: At stage 4 the ball of cells sinks into the uterus lining. Name this process.
hints: Name it: one word is enough.
parts.workedSolution: Implantation.

commonErrors.feedback: Sinking into the lining is a change of place: implantation. Differentiation is the change of job that follows it.

parts.stem: At stage 5 the cells form tissues and organs. Name this process.
hints: Name it: one word is enough.
parts.workedSolution: Differentiation.

commonErrors.feedback: Cells becoming different from one another to form tissues is a change of job: differentiation. Implantation was the change of place before it.

findTheMistake.stem:
Cara is asked: 'Under a microscope a sperm swam 4.8 mm in 3.0 minutes. Calculate its speed in mm per minute. [2]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is exactly the right equation. Line 2 puts the numbers in the wrong way round: it divides the time by the distance. Distance goes on top, so it should read 4.8 ÷ 3.0.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the two: the equation line stands. A quick check catches this every time — the unit asked for is millimetres per minute, so millimetres must be the thing being divided. Her answer of 0.63 is in minutes per millimetre.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Describe how an embryo develops from a zygote. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The zygote divides by mitosis to form a ball of identical cells.
The ball of cells implants in the lining of the uterus.
Then differentiation happens: the cells keep dividing to make more cells.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 describes more division, which is mitosis again. Differentiation is the cells becoming different from one another, taking on different jobs as tissues and organs form. Summer 2024 examiners found that, overall, candidates could not show what differentiation means.
correction: The zygote divides by mitosis to form a ball of identical cells.
The ball of cells implants in the lining of the uterus.
Then differentiation happens: the cells become different from one another.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of the three. The last mark needs the idea of cells becoming different: dividing again adds cells but changes no job.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aisling is asked: 'Describe what happens at fertilisation. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: A sperm reaches the egg in the oviduct.
The haploid nuclei of the sperm and the egg fuse.
This forms one diploid cell, called an embryo.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right, and so is 'one diploid cell'. But the single cell made at fertilisation is a zygote; it becomes an embryo only once it has divided into a ball of cells. Summer 2025 examiners saw this swap.
correction: A sperm reaches the egg in the oviduct.
The haploid nuclei of the sperm and the egg fuse.
This forms one diploid cell, called a zygote.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of the three. Count the cells: one cell is a zygote, a ball of many is an embryo.

prompts.prompt: What is a zygote, and how is it different from an embryo?
prompts.answer: A zygote is the single diploid cell formed when the haploid sperm and egg nuclei fuse. An embryo is the many cells that form once that zygote has divided by mitosis.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between implantation and differentiation?
prompts.answer: Implantation is a change of place: the ball of cells settles into the lining of the uterus. Differentiation is a change of job: the cells become different from one another to form tissues and organs.

prompts.prompt: Give three adaptations of a sperm cell, and the reason for each one.
prompts.answer: A haploid nucleus, so that fertilisation restores the diploid number; mitochondria, which release the energy for swimming; and a flagellum, which makes the sperm swim to the ovum.

prompts.prompt: Where does fertilisation take place, and what exactly happens there?
prompts.answer: In the oviduct. The haploid nucleus of the sperm and the haploid nucleus of the ovum fuse to give a diploid zygote.

prompts.prompt: How is the placenta adapted for diffusion? Give three points, each with its reason.
prompts.answer: The villi give a large surface area, so more diffusion happens at once; the barrier between the two blood supplies is thin, so the diffusion distance is short; and the good blood supply on both sides keeps the difference in concentration up.

prompts.prompt: Name the four substances the specification says cross the placenta, and say which way each one goes.
prompts.answer: Dissolved nutrients and oxygen cross to the foetus; carbon dioxide and urea cross from the foetus to the mother.

prompts.prompt: What do the umbilical cord, the amnion and the amniotic fluid each do?
prompts.answer: The umbilical cord carries blood, and so the substances in it, to and from the foetus. The amnion is the membrane around the foetus, and the amniotic fluid inside it cushions the foetus.

prompts.prompt: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many are in a sperm cell, and how many in the zygote it helps to form?
prompts.answer: 23 in the sperm, because a gamete is haploid, and 46 in the zygote, because the two haploid nuclei fuse and the zygote is diploid.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between a zygote and an embryo?
prompts.answer: A zygote is one cell; an embryo is a ball of many cells.

prompts.prompt: Implantation or differentiation: which is a change of place, and which of job?
prompts.answer: Implantation is a change of place, into the uterus lining; differentiation is a change of job.

prompts.prompt: Name the three adaptations of a sperm cell.
prompts.answer: A haploid nucleus, mitochondria to release energy, and a flagellum to swim.

prompts.prompt: Give the three features that suit the placenta to diffusion.
prompts.answer: Villi for a large surface area, a thin barrier, and a good blood supply.

prompts.prompt: What do the umbilical cord and the amniotic fluid each do?
prompts.answer: The cord carries blood to and from the foetus; the amniotic fluid cushions it.

prompts.prompt: In which part of the female body does fertilisation take place?
What is the single cell formed at fertilisation called?
